title: Teachers and Students 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Norman Fischer's reflections on his teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman, written for Mel's 80th birthday. Norman recalls the old Berkeley house on Dwight Way, with its attic zendo, Mel sitting at the head of the stairs every morning at five, and the plum tree and vegetable garden out back. Nomon adds comments on reading such stories without regret, keeping the seat warm for those who come later, and teachers being no different species from students. In discussion, Mary notes how few women appear in these early stories, and Nomon recalls Norman's wife Kathy taking her moldy okesa off the shelf at a Samish sesshin.

sentences.text: Good afternoon.
It's nice to experiment a little bit with their schedule.
We have on Fridays a little more practice after our usual Friday noon gig with talks and classes and maybe other rituals.
Originally, our entire schedule was just one evening; Wednesday evening has sort of all the fancy stuff.
So we'll start doing some fancy stuff on Friday afternoons and Saturdays too.
This afternoon, I'd like to reflect a little bit with you about teachers and students.
Once we're thinking about teachers in the Zen tradition, the obvious question is, what are they teaching?
If you have a teacher, usually the way we think about a teacher is that they're teaching something and the students are learning something.
There's some like object almost being passed from one to the other.
Is that the case with Zen teachers, or is that the case ever with any teacher?
It's sort of interesting to think about that.
The way I want to bring this up is mostly not with my words; I'm going to read to you a piece that my teacher wrote about his teacher.
Some reflections by Norman Fischer about his teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman written on the occasion of Mel's 80th birthday, which was last month.
I'm going to read you what he wrote about Mel and then reflect a little bit at the end, add some comments of my own.
It's unclear to me how long exactly these should last, but maybe we'll have a little bit of discussion if you have something to share or talk about from your experience or questions or what have you.
That's my plan.
We'll see this experiment, see how it goes, how it feels.
Here's what Norman wrote about Mel.
I study with Mel a bit and am very fond of Mel as well, and I'm sure Edie knows Mel also.
Mel is the avid of Berkeley's end center, where he has been sort of practicing steadily, doing a weekly schedule, just like we do, for forty years.
For forty years, yeah, so it's something.
Or is it?
Mel has been an inspiration, a guide, and a friend to me since I was a young man, as this is Norman's words.
I am one of the old Dwight Way crowds, which is the previous location for their center, which was just a house, just a house with an attic, a little zendo in the attic.
Recently I drove by that old place.
It is still there, but the yucca and the monkey puzzle trees in the front yard that were of modest size in the early nineteen seventies are large now, dwarfing the house.
I was struck at how different the place looked.
I attributed the difference to the fact that the practice, practice and spirit vacated the space so long ago.
Then the place had a simplicity and a dignity it doesn't seem to have now, a quiet but insistent presence.
Having felt these things then in the actual physical space and not feeling them now makes me understand better the virtue of Mel's teaching.
These are the words I would use to describe it: simplicity, dignity, and a quiet but insistent presence.

It seems to me that the main characteristic of Suzuki Roshi's teaching and of Soto Zen, which is the lineage we practice in, is faith in the practice, so faith in the practice and a steadiness and endurance to keep going with the practice no matter what.
As Dogen taught so profoundly, the practice is the enlightenment.
There is no enlightenment outside of practice.
In the early days, and I know it is the same now, it was clear without anyone needing to say so that this was the value most encouraged by Mel.
Back then there was sitting every morning at five a.m., and Mel was there every day, always on time.

Whether there was one person or two or three joining him and there were seldom more than three or four, he was always there, sitting in his place at the head of the stairs so that when you walked up those steep stairs to the attic you could see him first, just there, always there, motionless and quiet.
Dwight Way was a pretty busy street, and there was sometimes traffic by the end of the morning session, but traffic or no traffic, whatever was going on, there was steady, silent sitting.

Every day, week after week, month after month, and by now, decade after decade, though the location has changed and the years have sped by, I'm guessing that in this the practice remains the same and the spirit remains the same: just do the practice.
Have faith in the practice, come what may.
Be steady and endure.
Appreciate what is.
During the all-day sits, held once a month as I recall, there was frequently noise in the neighborhood, conversation, sometimes loud music.
We would sit through it, taking it as a benefit.
Practice is all-inclusive; it's not about having to be quiet.
Or, if it was too much, Mel would go out and talk to whomever it was, and somehow it would always be more quiet afterward.
The quiet after the noise was an even quieter quiet.
Which is a nice point about quiet, don't you think?
Not saying much, not explaining much.
That's how it was in those days.
There were no sesshin, which is like a long retreat.
No dokusan, a private interview with the teachers.
Nothing special or spectacular.
No large Buddhas on the altar.
Mel gave, I think, a talk on the all-day sittings, and maybe there was a weekly Dharma talk, but those events were always themselves very quiet.
Just part of the schedule.
I always found them moving and encouraging, but they were not charismatic or complicated or exciting.
Mel would speak pretty simply about our practice, very often bringing up sayings of the old teachers or Dogen, the old Zen teachers or Dogen.
And there was a simplicity to the way he expressed things.
Really, I can't remember much of what Mel said, but the general impression I had was a steadiness and wisdom and beauty, conviction, but lightly held.
Mel was a handsome fellow in those days, and still is at eighty, and the main message in those talks, at least the message I received, was just that: dignity and handsomeness of the teachings.
There was no insistence or pushing of any kind, and in a quiet voice Mel would just tell us something about the teachings.
He was very careful always in instructing us about how to walk, how to stand, how to eat, how to serve the meals and ring the bells, how to carry the stick and the zendo, and so on.
Physical carriage and form were important, and he would tell us about them, but not over and over again, maybe just once.
The sense of quiet and restraint, even about things that were clearly important, was very strong.
A phrase Mel would often use, maybe he still does, was the other side, by which he meant something like, things are done or meant this way, but there is always the other side.
You should do things slowly, but the other side is that sometimes you do them quickly.
Such and so is the case, but the other side is that it isn't.
I'm pretty sure Mel got this directly from Suzuki Roshi.
Though, as I recall, Mel didn't talk about Suzuki Roshi nearly as much then as he does now, and it seems very similar to me to Suzuki Roshi's not always so.
Maybe Suzuki Roshi said the other side.

I wouldn't be surprised, because I think much of what Mel said in those days and the ways in which he said it was directly inspired by Suzuki Roshi, whose presence I now imagine, looking back from the perspective of nearly forty years, was very much with Mel all the time.

However much he did or didn't consciously reference him, the sense that the practice, unlike anything we had previously thought of as religion, was more or less entirely a matter of physical presence, was very strong in those early days.
As I have said, though the place was simple, and not particularly Asian or Japanese in style or decor, you could really feel this.
There was a spareness in everything, an austerity, and also a beauty.
You'd walk into the house, and everything seemed quiet.
You didn't have to go upstairs to the Zendo.
Just approaching the front door, you felt the quiet.
It was a plain and ordinary modest Berkeley Victorian house, but it was always clean, things always in their places.

There were simple pictures on the walls, small ones except for a very large blue abstract painting by Mel, from his San Francisco beatnik artist days, a bulletin board by the front door with only a few necessary announcements on it, like the schedule.
The kitchen where we had coffee after morning zazen was always neat and ready.
Never any dishes left over from yesterday.
And there was a sense that everything was cared for, everything was considered and tended to.
There was no sense that things were displayed for effect.
Things were just there.
They were useful.
They were simple.
They were there.
No effort whatsoever to impress anyone, or even to express if this was a Zen place, or even a Buddhist place.
Probably it was clear that it was.
I'm sure there were pieces of calligraphy or Zen art on the walls, so I can't remember now.
There was a library with Buddhist books.
But the feeling was that no effort was being made to emphasize this point.
It was as if everything expressed the practice.
That is, that things were there to be used and cared for, not to make a point.
You could feel this.

Outside in the backyard, where Mel spent a considerable amount of time, there was an extensive garden, whose main feature was an old plum tree that had spread out over the years, so its branches seemed to reach everywhere.
When it was in flower, it dominated the yard.
You'd have to walk off and bent over to avoid the profusion of white blossoms that seemed to be everywhere.
Blossoms and the bees that went into them.
Otherwise there were veggies, a serious number of veggies.
Mel was an organic gardener, something of an early expert in the field.
He worked hard growing vegetables for the Sangha.
The backyard was quite extensive and very full.
It seemed a world in itself.
Although the neighbor's house and yard weren't far away, they seemed far away.
There were always projects afoot in that yard that we engaged during work periods at the monthly day-long sittings.
Work period and work practice were always central to the Zen note life.
And Mel usually led the work and usually knew exactly what he wanted done.
My training there taught me that Zen and work were synonymous.
Mel modeled the way of working that was exemplary: steady effort over time, without too much exertion, always accomplished with tremendous focus and in silence.
In the early nineteen seventies, when my life more or less fell apart, I was in a state of confusion and near dysfunction.
Mel and Liz took me into their lives, into the healing space of the Zen-do environs.
Mel didn't say much to me, didn't offer advice or ask me to talk much about what my problems were.
But he opened the house to me, gave me a room to sleep in, and every day there was work, sitting, simple meals.
Little by little, I began to come back to myself.
Often we had lunch out in the garden under the plum tree.
We drank cups of delicious green tea, ate good dark bread and cheese, and said almost nothing.
In those days, there was a family feeling in the Zen-do community.
There weren't many of us, but we were all dedicated and steady in our practice, which for all of us was the center of our lives.
As a teacher and guide, and also as a person nearly twenty years older than most of us, Mel was somewhat aloof, distinctly in a different position, yet also warm and close.
Without intervening much, he encouraged and supported us all in our various efforts to figure out who we were and what we were supposed to be doing.
I'm not sure we really realized this then, but looking back on it now, it seems pretty clear.
My dear old friend Alan Liu was active in the group too and became what was called the director.
He and Mel were very close.

And when Open Books published our first books of poetry, so Norman and Alan's first books of poetry, Mel encouraged us to give what was our first reading ever downstairs in the basement of the Zen-do.
A lot of people came, and for courage we both, well, I speak for myself, got pretty drunk and gave what we thought were brilliant readings, but were probably pretty stupid and self-indulgent.
But the point is that Mel allowed this, encouraged us, and didn't complain about how it turned out.
Alan died suddenly early this year, and Mel and Liz had a gathering at their house for people from those days.

To recall Alan and those times long ago, the beginnings of things are always special, even though as things go on they usually get better, more developed, fairer, more competent, more effective, larger, and so on.
But the beginning always has a special character, a simplicity, a pungency.
It makes me think of someone who will be giving a talk forty years from now, sitting here.
Back in those days, I didn't know Suzuki Roshi.
I was actually around when he was alive and functioning before his illness, but I was too blind and ignorant to realize that I had a chance to meet a great teacher, and I ought to take it.
Instead, I was wrapped up in my own thoughts and needs and didn't feel I had any use for a teacher.
Mel appealed to me because he didn't call himself a teacher or even come across as one.
He was just a priest leading the practice, just there, not somebody you would somehow get credit for having known, and people didn't make any fuss over him.
And because Mel didn't mention Suzuki Roshi very much, I barely knew he existed.
I remember a notice of his funeral appearing one day on the small bulletin board by the front door, a modest notice as I recall.
It didn't seem like anything I'd want to go to; I didn't know the guy, and that's the point of attending a funeral anyway.
Clearly, though, the people who knew Suzuki Roshi and were able to practice with him were deeply moved by him.
Probably each one of them carried away with them their own private Suzuki Roshi, their own view from the standpoint of their karma of who Suzuki Roshi was and what his life expressed.
They say that when a good teacher gives a Dharma talk, each listener comes away with a different talk, a talk given just for them.
And I'm sure this was also true of Suzuki Roshi's whole sense of life and practice.
Each one had their own Suzuki Roshi.

It seems to me that Mel's Suzuki Roshi embodied the qualities I've been speaking about: the quiet, the simplicity, the modesty, and the supportiveness without saying or doing much, the simple beauty, the devotion to work, and the steady daily practice.

Though I'm a generation away, I have heard the Suzuki Roshi stories, met and studied with most of Suzuki Roshi's disciples, read the talks, heard the tapes, bowed monthly and yearly at memorial services.
So I also feel I know Suzuki Roshi, and he does seem to me to be very like Mel.
A good student takes in a great teacher and makes him completely his own.
I think Mel has done this with his teacher.
Probably I have not done this with mine.
Maybe it's because I'm not a devoted enough student, or maybe I haven't gotten over my excessive interest in my own thoughts and needs.
Or maybe Mel is not a great enough teacher.
Probably, though, it is none of these.
Probably it's because times have changed and we all build on what has gone before.
So though what was possible in the beginning—the kind of inspiring devotion to a teacher and full incorporation of his or her into one's own life—is not possible after a while, I don't know.
But I do know that I have not digested Mel's teachings in the same way that he digested his teacher.
I remain, for better or worse, myself, with my own inclinations and interests.
My style of practice is probably not that much like Mel's or even Suzuki Roshi's and comes out of my own necessities more than anything else.
I left Berkeley because I wanted to do monastic practice at Tassajara.
Just before I entered the monastery, I married and we had children right away.
They had twins, too, which complicated things and caused us to remain residents of San Francisco Zen Center for twenty-five years or so longer than we had planned.
I was ordained as a priest a little later by then abbot Dick Baker in 1980 with my wife Kathy, with our three-year-old twin sons looking on with a strange, gleeful amusement.

And after I finished my term as abbot of the Zen Center in 2000, I began the Everyday Zen Foundation, a network of Zen communities and associated projects which now involves a lot of talented and interesting people who practice Zen together with me all over the place in various ways, some not even quite identifiable as Zen, though many of the groups are local Soto Zen groups, quite like the old Berkeley Zen Center.
So unlike Mel, I travel constantly and have no place that I can take care of, meaning no temple where he is every day.
My way of practice emphasizes committed, disciplined, daily sitting, but sitting usually at home.
None of our places offer daily sitting, along with time for sesshin or weekend retreats.

Still in the grip of my old writing habit, I continue to write poetry and prose books, and my practice emphasizes, in a way I don't think Mel's or Suzuki Roshi's does, written expression of study and cultural involvement.
I've also found that expression and communication and close personal relationships with students without much reserve is at the heart of my practice.
This seems to come naturally to me.
I don't know if I could avoid it even if I wanted to.
I'm not that much on work.
Not that I don't do it or don't believe in it; I do work a bit around the house, but left to my own devices, I will read, write, or exercise.
She says, "goof off," but not here.
I try to take care of the physical world, but I guess I don't do it very well.

But I hope, and I believe, that I have internalized the faithfulness to simple practice, to know Phil's constancy and endurance over time that I learned at Mel's place, and that I believe is at the heart of Suzuki Roshi's way as well, just to practice and be willing to share practice in a simple way with others.
No big secret teachings, no profound enlightenment, just simple, stupid, Soto Zen, every day.
I am, I think this is the case, Mel's first Dharma heir.
We completed the Shiho Dharma transmission ceremonies October twenty-fifth, a full moon night in 1988, at Tassajara.
A wonderful experience for both of us, but we probably stumbled through it without knowing exactly how to do it.

Since then, I have transmitted the Dharma to eleven priests, some of them Mel's disciples, in addition to being students of mine, and I did the ceremonies with his blessing as a way of helping him out.
Some were priests ordained by others who needed help with the last stages of their training, and some were people I ordained and trained.
The last time I did the ceremonies, March of 2009, I had Mel's picture on the transmission altar.

In this picture, Mel is in his in-sivis, wearing a rakusu, close-up, body turned to one side, smiling wonderfully, looking as if he's about to come forward from his chair towards the viewer to say hello or give a hug.
It's a very friendly, very informal picture, and it was nice to have it with us, guiding the process along, which he's described to me in this process a little bit.
It's a very long, long ceremony.
It takes a week, actually.
It's like a week-long ceremony.
And a lot of it, for whatever reason, has to be done in the middle of the night, so it's kind of a grueling sort of thing.
A little more from Norman, and then I'll make a few comments.
What, after all, is a Zen teacher, and what role is he or she supposed to have in the life of a committed student?
As I've said, I don't know whether this is a reflection of Mel's character or mine, but Mel has not been a guide or advisor to me in the usual way.
Even though we practiced together every day, we didn't talk very much for many years.
And when I was at San Francisco Zen Center, across the bay, we didn't see each other very often.
So I've not sought out his advice generally, although, of course, sometimes I have, when I needed advice.
It seems to me my relationship with him is deeper and more mysterious than this.
In a way, I don't need his advice, because I know how he thinks, know what he would say.
I have internalized his view in this way.
Though, of course, I recognize that he might not agree, that the Mel in me, the real Mel to me, may not agree with the other Mel, who thinks he's Mel, and who others call Mel.
But that doesn't mean I don't need that other exterior Mel.
I do.
In fact, without saying anything or doing anything in relation to me directly, he helps me out a lot, just by being in the world, continuing to do what he has always done.
His mysterious activity in the actual physical world across the bay, over there in Berkeley, is a continuous support for me.
And if it should happen he dies before I do, I will miss him a lot, even though I don't see him that often.
The influence of a Zen teacher on a committed student is very powerful.
It is ordinary and extraordinary at the same time, as I understand that the teacher doesn't know what he is doing.
That is, he doesn't scope out the student, decide what is needed, and then proceed sneakily and subtly to make sure the student gets it.
Instead, the teacher just continues the practice with a benevolent wish for the student.
Between them something deeply important and transformative occurs, but neither one of them is in charge of it.
It just happens, somehow, between them.
Because there is a willingness for it to happen, because they are willing to go on with their practice, come what may, because they have faith and trust and courage.
In any case, this is what I have come to understand from my Dogen studies and from my life.
This is what I have faith in after nearly forty years of continuous practice with Mel.
Isn't that beautiful?
It's hard not to read that without crying.
So I think it's wonderful to learn a little bit about the teachers who have gone before.
To be careful, though, not to indulge in our golden years habit that we sometimes have, not to feel like we somehow missed out, should have been there, shouldn't have done the things we did.
If only I had been unemployed and a Zen bum in my twenties.
Everything would be great now, which is kind of what they were.
Actually, he talks about Mel being older, so I'm amused now, because the time that Norman is writing about, Norman was in his early twenties, and Mel was in his early forties, which I am now.
When I started studying with Norman, I was in my early twenties, and Norman was in his early forties.
So there's a beautiful way that it just seems to go around.
So anyway, to appreciate the effort, the steady effort over time, that directly or indirectly, and it seems in a way an obvious sort of linear narrative.

If Sojun Mel Weitsman hadn't shown up every morning at five in the morning in that attic in Berkeley, Norman wouldn't have started practicing, maybe I wouldn't have started practicing, maybe who knows what would have happened.
But actually, the story of how things unfold is much more mysterious than that, we know.
So to read these stories without regret or jealousy, but with warmth and appreciation and love, so that we can be inspired to keep our practice steady for those ones coming after us.
That's something that Jeff McKenna has told me and the sangha a few times recently, which I really appreciate.

I think he learned this from the Native American cultures that he hangs out with, that our purpose being here in the Dharma Hall or in our lives is not so much to get something for ourselves or solve anything, but to take care of it while we have it, to keep the seat warm for those who are coming later.
And it helps us to understand that if we understand the people who came before a little bit, keeping the seat warm for us.

And the other thing I appreciate about this piece is also its understanding of how all traditions change and adapt, that Norman recognizes that he does not really teach in the exact same style as his teacher or the much-esteemed Suzuki Roshi, who everyone loves to love.
And that's okay.
And that's different in a way and the same in a way.
And so we're free.
We're freed up.
We can adapt things in Bellingham as we see fit.
There's a great beauty to the simplicity of the kind of practice that we're doing.
But of course, without any instructions or intro to Zen classes, you're probably not going to have more than four people, does that know?
And there's nothing wrong with that.
But we also can feel confident that it's okay for us to have some instruction and some classes and interviews and so on and teachers.

Maybe we have the opportunity to reach more than four people, and that's wonderful too, so long as the basis of that reaching is not reaching, is staying in our seats, is appreciating also that spirit and staying quietly in the attic day after day without any sort of idea of getting something or improving something.

And they say that the Zen tradition, you can learn a lot about the Zen tradition by reading books, and we're working on juicing up our library because they tell us, and Mary told me I think, that a very large number of people come to Dharma practice in the West through their reading or book and word and concept culture.
But that can only go so far.
They say the Zen tradition is passed on from warm hand to warm hand, from warm hand to warm hand.
That's the only way it can be passed on, and it can only be understood through the living of it.
It's something that can be cognized and talked about, and it's something beyond that.
And somehow when people have been practicing for a long time with some steadiness, somehow in their words they can remind us of what's beyond words, like this piece of Norman's does.
It's just a bunch of words on a paper that I printed out from the internet, which didn't even exist in 1970, and yet it touches something deep inside us.
That's beyond words.
And at one historical note, you might have noticed that all these early stories mention about a thousand men and about two women.
You notice that?
I don't know if my wife would have been so acquiescent if I took in a troubled twenty-year-old Zen student into her house.
And I don't actually even know Mel's wife, even though I've practiced with Mel several times.
I didn't even know her name until this piece.
And in this piece Norman mentions her.
He said Mel and Liz took him in.
But other times he's talked about that time and Liz, so I think there's some things not to romanticize so much about early Zen.
I think it was very much a product of its time in that way that it was understood in a fairly chauvinistic and macho sort of way.
And probably the woman who could stick it out were pretty tough, took on a lot of that energy just to hang in there.
So I'm glad they were a little bit beyond that, and a little bit beyond also sort of tremendous romanticization.
They had about Zen and enlightenment, that if you gave up everything and just sat zaz until your butt was falling off, great thing would happen to you.
We don't think that so much anymore.
We understand practice as a part of a healthy life that needs a fuller expression to be real valuable to us and the world.
And so nobody lives here.
Occasionally I fantasize about that.
There's a couple of rental houses on the property.
Wouldn't that be wonderful?
But it would also be a fair amount of trouble.
Because what happens then is the people who don't live here feel like lesser beings than the people who do live here, and all kinds of things happen.
Maybe we'll get to that.
We'll see.
It'll be good trouble if we do it.
So I think that's all I intended to say.
It's brief for once, rare for me.
So we have a few minutes.
Does anyone want to say anything about what that brought up for you or your experience with teachers and students, of which we are all both, really?
That's the other point I want to make.
The other thing about early Zen, which I'm happy that we're a little bit over, is we don't understand teachers to be sort of a different species, you know, sort of a special species.

And if you read the introduction to Zen Mind Beginner's Mind, the introduction by some of the comments from Trudy Dixon who edited it, or sort of outrageously that way, there's this part about how Zen roshis are sort of like on another planet.
And much as we deeply appreciate and understand that we need teachers, we need people who have been practicing a long time to remind us they're not a different species.
They're human beings just like us.
And there's a sort of abjugation of responsibility in that too, in that understanding that we think, well, it's the teacher's problem.
It's not my problem.
Take care of my life, you know.
So I think now we understand that we're all students and we're all teachers, and that takes a great weight off my back, I can tell you.
So that's good.
But anyway, that's the last last point I want to make.
Anyone want to add anything or say anything?
Just wondering how that can, what I normally think of, I think it's a story, something like that.
You have to put up a different type of thought because it's not about you.
How do you consider that thinking your own thoughts?
But if it's wrong to spend that much time thinking your own thoughts, you won't be able to write a fiction novel.
That's a good question.
Part of what he was doing is being a little bit sardonic, just in his appreciation for his teacher, sort of humbling himself a little bit.
So I think that's part of it.
But I think you're making an important point.
Part of it here, I think, is that through spiritual practice, we can understand our thoughts and our thinking process in a wider context, you know what I mean?

There's a way that when we're a little bit too involved, I think what he's pointing out is there's a way that we can become a little too involved with our thinking, as if our thinking was like the whole of us.
And when we're strongly self-identified with our thinking, then your entire being and self-esteem and happiness is like riding on this thinking process, you know what I mean?

So therefore, if you can write a good story, if it's a good story, you're a good person, if you can't get it together, write a good story, you're a disaster and it's a failure, and things are terrible, you know what I mean?
And so if we can sort of understand that thinking process is just one of the tools available for us in a wider context that's sort of beyond thinking, you know what I mean?
That our actual life is kind of like beyond thinking.

And thinking arises, and sometimes that's the story, but sometimes we realize, you know what, it'd be better right now just to let that drop, you know, and enjoy the sunset or be with my family or my friends, you know what I mean?

So I think that's kind of what he's pointing out, that there's a way that being too involved with our thinking and our priorities is sort of self-defeating because it sort of creates this sort of self-identified, sort of confused gloss on everything, you know what I mean?
And this is, I think, why so many artists are in Iraq, you know what I mean?
You know what I mean?
They die young from depression and terrible problems because they're a little too much, you know, this is the whole thing, you know?
So that's a really good question though, and he does say that in a little bit of an off-way there, so yeah, nobody's perfect.
Yeah, thanks.
Good point.
Yeah, Mary.
You mentioned the fact that women weren't a big part of that story that you were talking about.
I'm interested in the fact that Norman's wife is such a complete mystery to us.
I mean, this isn't more of a statement than a question, but I only recently been listening to...
She came to sesshin with us two years ago, and she's coming this year also, actually.
So we'll see her at Samish.
Well, I know Cathy some, you know, not super well, but I know her, and yeah, she just decided that she was really a lot more interested in expressing dharma through raising their kids and teaching.
She's a teacher, teaches middle school science and is a great lover of science and teaching science.

And she's also, and this is kind of part of the difference between Norman and Cathy and Mel and Liz maybe, she also early on decided she needed some boundaries, you know, between her and Norman's kind of growing teaching gig.
And my wife is this way too.

So yeah, so, you know, early on they got a separate line, like a separate phone line, like I later did, and, you know, it was kind of frowned on to bug Cathy and to, you know, you should meet Norman in kind of an organized way and not go knocking on their door.

But yeah, so she did kind of set down formal practice for a long time, and then when she came to our sesshin at Samish two years ago, she had had her the formal Zenro of the Okesa like on the shelf for a long time, twenty years maybe, and she took it out and it was all moldy.
And it kind of like started, it was sort of like falling apart, you know, they had like hung it up and smelled bad.

verbatim.text: Good afternoon. It's nice to experiment a little bit with their schedule. then the obvious question is, well, what are they teaching? If you have a teacher, usually the way we think about a teacher is that they're teaching something and the students are learning something. There's some like object almost being passed from one to the other. And so is that the case with Zen teachers or is that the case ever with any teacher? It's sort of interesting to think about that. And the way I want to bring this up, mostly it is not with my words, I'm going to read to you a piece that my teacher wrote about his teacher.

Some reflections by Norman Fischer about his teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman written on the occasion of Mel's 80th birthday, which was last month. So I'm going to read you what he wrote about Mel and then reflect a little bit at the end, add some comments of my own. And then it's unclear to me how long exactly these should last, but maybe we'll have a little bit of discussion if you have something to share or talk about from your experience or questions or what have you. So that's my plan.

We'll see this experiment, see how it goes, how it feels. So here's what Norman wrote about Mel. And I study with Mel a bit and am very fond of Mel as well, and I'm sure Edie knows Mel also. Mel is the avid of Berkeley's end center, where he has been sort of practicing steadily, doing a weekly schedule, just like we do, for 40 years. For 40 years, yeah, so it's something.

Or is it? Mel has been an inspiration, a guide, and a friend to me since I was a young man, as this is Norman's words. I am one of the old Dwight Way crowds, which is the previous location for their center, which was just a house, just a house with an attic, a little zendo in the attic. Recently I drove by that old place.

It is still there, but the yucca and the monkey puzzle trees in the front yard that were of modest size in the early 1970s are large now, dwarfing the house. I was struck at how different the place looked. I attributed the difference to the fact that the practice, practice and spirit vacated the space so long ago. Then the place had a simplicity and a dignity it doesn't seem to have now, a quiet but insistent presence.

Having felt these things then in the actual physical space and not feeling them now makes me understand better the virtue of Mel's teaching. These are the words I would use to describe it. Simplicity, dignity, and a quiet but insistent presence. It seems to me that the main characteristic of Suzuki Roshi's teaching and of Soto Zen, which is the lineage we practice in,

is faith in the practice, so faith in the practice and a steadiness and endurance to keep going with the practice no matter what. As Dogen taught so profoundly, the practice is the enlightenment. There is no enlightenment outside of practice. In the early days, and I know it is the same now, it was clear without anyone needing to say so

that this was the value most encouraged by Mel. Back then there was sitting every morning at 5 a.m. and Mel was there every day, always on time. Whether there was one person or two or three joining him and there were seldom more than three or four, he was always there, sitting in his place at the head of the stairs so that when you walked up those steep stairs to the attic

you could see him first, just there, always there, motionless and quiet. Dwight Way was a pretty busy street and there was sometimes traffic by the end of the morning session, but traffic or no traffic, whatever was going on, there was steady, silent sitting. Every day, week after week, month after month. And by now, decade after decade,

though the location has changed and the years have sped by, I'm guessing that in this the practice remains the same and the spirit remains the same, just do the practice. Have faith in the practice, come what may. Be steady and endure. Appreciate what is. During the all-day sits, held once a month as I recall, there was frequently noise in the neighborhood,

conversation, sometimes loud music. We would sit through it, taking it as a benefit. Practice is all-inclusive, it's not about having to be quiet. Or, if it was too much, Mel would go out and talk to whomever it was and somehow it would always be more quiet afterward. The quiet after the noise was an even quieter quiet. Which is a nice point about quiet, don't you think? Not saying much, not explaining much.

That's how it was in those days. There were no sesshin, which is like a long retreat. No dokusan, a private interview with the teachers. Nothing special or spectacular. No large Buddhas on the altar. Mel gave, I think, a talk on the all-day sittings and maybe there was a weekly Dharma talk, but those events were always themselves very quiet.

Just part of the schedule. I always found them moving and encouraging, but they were not charismatic or complicated or exciting. Mel would speak pretty simply about our practice. Very often bringing up sayings of the old teachers or Dogen, the old Zen teachers or Dogen. And there was a simplicity to the way he expressed things. Really, I can't remember much of what Mel said,

but the general impression I had was a steadiness and wisdom and beauty. Conviction, but lightly held. Mel was a handsome fellow in those days, and still is at 80, and the main message in those talks, at least the message I received, was just that. Dignity and handsomeness of the teachings.

There was no insistence or pushing of any kind, and in a quiet voice Mel would just tell us something about the teachings. He was very careful always in instructing us about how to walk, how to stand, how to eat, how to serve the meals and ring the bells, how to carry the stick and the zendo, and so on. Physical carriage and form were important,

and he would tell us about them, but not over and over again, maybe just once. The sense of quiet and restraint, even about things that were clearly important, was very strong. A phrase Mel would often use, maybe he still does, was the other side, by which he meant something like,

things are done or meant this way, but there is always the other side. You should do things slowly, but the other side is that sometimes you do them quickly. Such and so is the case, but the other side is that it isn't. I'm pretty sure Mel got this directly from Suzuki Roshi. Though, as I recall, Mel didn't talk about Suzuki Roshi

nearly as much then as he does now, and it seems very similar to me to Suzuki Roshi's not always so. Maybe Suzuki Roshi said the other side. I wouldn't be surprised, because I think much of what Mel said in those days and the ways in which he said it was directly inspired by Suzuki Roshi,

whose presence I now imagine, looking back from the perspective of nearly 40 years, was very much with Mel all the time. However much he did or didn't consciously reference him, the sense that the practice, unlike anything we had previously thought of as religion, was more or less entirely a matter of physical presence, was very strong in those early days.

As I have said, though the place was simple, and not particularly Asian or Japanese in style or decor, you could really feel this. There was a spareness in everything, an austerity, and also a beauty. You'd walk into the house, and everything seemed quiet. You didn't have to go upstairs to the Zendo. Just approaching the front door, you felt the quiet.

It was a plain and ordinary modest Berkeley Victorian house, but it was always clean, things always in their places. There were simple pictures on the walls, small ones except for a very large blue abstract painting by Mel, from his San Francisco beatnik artist days, a bulletin board by the front door with only a few necessary announcements on it,

like the schedule. The kitchen where we had coffee after morning zazen was always neat and ready. Never any dishes left over from yesterday. And there was a sense that everything was cared for, everything was considered and tended to. There was no sense that things were displayed for effect. Things were just there.

They were useful. They were simple. They were there. No effort whatsoever to impress anyone, or even to express if this was a Zen place, or even a Buddhist place. Probably it was clear that it was. I'm sure there were pieces of calligraphy or Zen art on the walls,

so I can't remember now. There was a library with Buddhist books. But the feeling was that no effort was being made to emphasize this point. It was as if everything expressed the practice. That is, that things were there to be used and cared for, not to make a point. You could feel this. Outside in the backyard, where Mel spent a considerable amount of time,

there was an extensive garden, whose main feature was an old plum tree that had spread out over the years, so its branches seemed to reach everywhere. When it was in flower, it dominated the yard. You'd have to walk off and bent over to avoid the profusion of white blossoms that seemed to be everywhere. Blossoms and the bees that went into them. Otherwise there were veggies, a serious number of veggies.

Mel was an organic gardener, something of an early expert in the field. He worked hard growing vegetables for the Sangha. The backyard was quite extensive and very full. It seemed a world in itself. Although the neighbor's house and yard weren't far away, they seemed far away. There were always projects afoot in that yard

that we engaged during work periods at the monthly day-long sittings. Work period and work practice were always central to the Zen note life. And Mel usually led the work and usually knew exactly what he wanted done. My training there taught me that Zen and work were synonymous. Mel modeled the way of working that was exemplary, steady effort over time, without too much exertion, always accomplished with tremendous focus and in silence. In the early 1970s, when my life more or less fell apart,

I was in a state of confusion and near dysfunction. Mel and Liz took me into their lives, into the healing space of the Zen-do environs. Mel didn't say much to me, didn't offer advice or ask me to talk much about what my problems were. But he opened the house to me, gave me a room to sleep in, and every day there was work, sitting, simple meals. Little by little, I began to come back to myself.

Often we had lunch out in the garden under the plum tree. We drank cups of delicious green tea, ate good dark bread and cheese, and said almost nothing. In those days, there was a family feeling in the Zen-do community. There weren't many of us, but we were all dedicated and steady in our practice, which for all of us was the center of our lives. As a teacher and guide, and also as a person

nearly 20 years older than most of us, Mel was somewhat aloof, distinctly in a different position, yet also warm and close. Without intervening much, he encouraged and supported us all in our various efforts to figure out who we were and what we were supposed to be doing. I'm not sure we really realized this then, but looking back on it now, it seems pretty clear.

My dear old friend Alan Liu was active in the group too and became what was called the director. He and Mel were very close. And when Open Books published our first books of poetry, so Norman and Alan's first books of poetry, Mel encouraged us to give what was our first reading ever downstairs in the basement of the Zen-do. A lot of people came, and for courage we both,

well, I speak for myself, got pretty drunk and gave what we thought were brilliant readings, but were probably pretty stupid and self-indulgent. But the point is that Mel allowed this, encouraged us, and didn't complain about how it turned out. Alan died suddenly early this year, and Mel and Liz had a gathering at their house for people from those days.

To recall Alan and those times long ago, the beginnings of things are always special, even though as things go on they usually get better, more developed, fairer, more competent, more effective, larger and so on. But the beginning always has a special character, a simplicity, a pungency. Makes me think of someone will be giving a talk

40 years from now sitting here. Back in those days, you know. I didn't know Suzuki Roshi. I was actually around when he was alive and functioning before his illness, but I was too blind and ignorant to realize that I had a chance to meet a great teacher, and I ought to take it.

Instead I was wrapped up in my own thoughts and needs and didn't feel I had any use for a teacher. Mel appealed to me because he didn't call himself a teacher or even come across as one. He was just a priest leading the practice, just there, not somebody you would somehow get credit for having known, and people didn't make any fuss over him. And because Mel didn't mention Suzuki Roshi very much,

I barely knew he existed. I remember a notice of his funeral appearing one day on the small bulletin board by the front door, a modest notice as I recall. It didn't seem like anything I'd want to go to, didn't know the guy, and that's the point of attending a funeral anyway. Clearly though, the people who knew Suzuki Roshi

Probably each one of them carried away with them their own private Suzuki Roshi, their own view from the standpoint of their karma of who Suzuki Roshi was and what his life expressed. And I'm sure this was also true of Suzuki Roshi's whole sense of life and practice. Each one had their own Suzuki Roshi. It seems to me that Mel's Suzuki Roshi embodied the qualities I've been speaking about, the quiet, the simplicity, the modesty, and the supportiveness without saying or doing much, the simple beauty, the devotion to work,

and the steady daily practice. Though I'm a generation away, I have heard the Suzuki Roshi stories, met and studied with most of Suzuki Roshi's disciples, read the talks, heard the tapes, bowed monthly and yearly at memorial services. A good student takes in a great teacher and makes him completely his own. I think Mel has done this with his teacher. Probably I have not done this with mine. Maybe it's because I'm not a devoted enough student or maybe I haven't gotten over my excessive interest in my own thoughts and needs. Or maybe Mel is not a great enough teacher.

Probably, though, it is none of these. Probably it's because times have changed and we all build on what has gone before. So though what was possible in the beginning, the kind of inspiring devotion to a teacher and full incorporation of his or her into one's own life is not possible after a while, I don't know. My style of practice is probably not that much like Mel's or even Suzuki Roshi's and comes out of my own necessities more than anything else. I left Berkeley because I wanted to do

with my wife Kathy, with our three-year-old twin sons looking on with a strange, gleeful amusement. and close personal relationships with students without much reserve is at the heart of my practice. This seems to come naturally to me. I don't know if I could avoid it even if I wanted to. She says, goof off, but not here. I try to take care of the physical world, but I guess I don't do it very well. just to practice and be willing to share practice in a simple way with others. No big secret teachings, no profound enlightenment, just simple, stupid, Soto Zen, every day. took on a lot of that energy just to hang in there. So I'm glad they were a little bit beyond that. And a little bit beyond also sort of tremendous romanticization. from Trudy Dixon who edited it, or sort of outrageously that way, there's this part about how Zen roshis are sort of like on another planet. And much as we deeply appreciate and understand that we need teachers, we need people who have been practicing a long time to remind us

they're not a different species. They're human beings just like us. And there's a sort of abjugation of responsibility in that too, in that understanding that we think, well, it's the teacher's problem. It's not my problem. Take care of my life, you know.

what I normally think of, I think it's a story, something like that. You have to put up, a different type of thought because it's not about you. How do you consider that thinking your own thoughts?

So I think that's part of it. But I think you're making an important point. Part of it here, I think, is that through spiritual practice, we can understand our thoughts and our thinking process in a wider context, you know what I mean? There's a way that

when we're a little bit too involved, I think what he's pointing out is there's a way that we can become a little too involved with our thinking, as if our thinking was like the whole of us. And when we're strongly self-identified with our thinking, then your entire

being and self-esteem and happiness is like riding on this thinking process, you know what I mean? just to let that drop, you know, and enjoy the sunset or be with my family or my friends, you know what I mean?
